Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

Negative Appraisals.value: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
I can't trust that I will do the right thing

issues.explanation: The Memory node is internally strained: intense guilt, rage, and overwhelming grief on recall can co-occur, but selecting all three as core recall responses without any memory-content item suggests an over-broad affect cluster rather than a coherent memory profile.

Cross-node coherence is weak between Negative Appraisals and Memory: 'No Accountability' aligns with anger/rage, but 'Contamination' is more typical of sexual trauma or morally violating trauma and is not well supported by the rest of the assault profile.

For an adult male assaulted in a non-sexual assault profile, 'Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened' is clinically hard to reconcile unless other items indicate sexual assault, bodily violation, or washing/avoidance themes, which are absent here.

For an adult male assault survivor, intense guilt, overwhelming grief, and feeling dirty/contaminated can occur, but this specific combination is hard to reconcile without any accompanying sexual-assault-type cues elsewhere in the profile. The contamination appraisal in particular pulls toward a trauma meaning not supported by the other selected items.

Within the Memory node, 'Guilt on Recall' and 'Grief on Recall' are not contradictory, but paired with predominantly visual memories they imply a complex emotional recall profile that would usually be echoed in appraisals more directly tied to guilt/loss. Instead, the appraisal set emphasizes injustice, incapacity, and contamination, which do not form a tight thematic cluster.

The formulation has a strong Negative Appraisals → Threat link, so appraisals should plausibly explain the threat items. 'No Longer Capable' fits hypervigilance/feeling unsafe, but 'No Accountability' mainly reflects injustice and does not clearly drive 'Safe Zone Only' or 'Startle to Movement.' 'Contamination' especially does not map well to the selected threat items, making the appraisal-to-threat pattern clinically incoherent.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, Self-Blame and No Accountability point in different directions of responsibility for the assault. A patient can feel both guilt and anger, but stated this strongly they suggest opposing appraisals about who is responsible.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences
issues.explanation: Memory item Guilt on Recall reinforces self-blame, which increases the inconsistency with the concurrent appraisal that perpetrators are the ones who should face consequences. The profile mixes strong perpetrator-focused blame with strong self-focused blame without a coherent bridge in the selected items.

The negative appraisal items are dominated by external blame/injustice ('the people responsible have faced no consequences', 'what happened was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it'), which fits an assault survivor, but this sits poorly with 'When I remember the event I feel intense guilt.' Intense guilt usually implies some degree of self-blame, responsibility, or perceived preventability. While mixed emotions are possible, this combination is clinically hard to reconcile here because the appraisal node contains no corresponding self-blaming belief and instead consistently locates responsibility outside the patient.

Within the Memory node, 'Guilt on Recall' is not well aligned with the other memory qualities selected ('mostly pictures or images' and 'can't put the event into words'), which describe sensory, poorly elaborated trauma memory. Those memory-form items plausibly link to threat, but guilt-on-recall points to a different meaning structure that is not supported by the selected negative appraisals. Given the formulation's strongest active pathway is Negative Appraisals → Threat, the absence of guilt-based appraisals makes the guilt memory item feel disconnected from the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Kwame, a 50-year-old plumber who had built his reputation over three decades on steady hands and reliable judgement, could no longer remember what it felt like to be sure of himself. The assault had happened eighteen months ago, on a Tuesday afternoon, in the basement boiler room of a low-rise apartment building he’d serviced for years. A tenant, high on something volatile and furious over a water shut-off notice, had cornered him by the furnace. Kwame remembered the man’s shadow first, then the crowbar swinging in an arc he could still see when he closed his eyes—a frozen image, metallic and stark, without any words attached. He had tried to report it, had filed a police report and given a statement, but the tenant had a cousin in the district attorney’s office and nothing ever came of it. No charges, no apology, no acknowledgment that the world had shifted under his feet. What remained was the picture: the crowbar, the stained concrete floor, the way his own hands had come up too late.

That image returned at odd moments—while driving, while sitting at the dinner table with his wife, while trying to fall asleep. It was a silent movie, playing without narration, and Kwame could not find the language to explain it. When his wife asked what had happened that day, he would say “I was attacked” and then stop, because the words felt hollow, as if the real event existed only in pictures that could not be translated. The guilt came with the image. Not guilt about what he had done—he had done nothing wrong—but a deep, ugly feeling that he should have been faster, stronger, smarter, that he should have seen it coming. He would lie awake at three in the morning replaying the moment, trying to rewrite it so that the crowbar missed, so that he ducked, so that the outcome was different. The sleep that had once come easily now required a careful ritual: checking the locks twice, sleeping on the side of the bed closest to the door, keeping a heavy wrench under the mattress. Even then he would startle awake at the sound of a car door or a creaking floorboard, heart hammering as if the man were standing in the bedroom doorway.

The world had shrunk. Kwame now felt safe only in three places: his own home, his mother’s house in the next suburb, and the small hardware store where he bought supplies—and even the hardware store had become uncertain after the day a customer had reached suddenly for a shelf behind him and Kwame had dropped to a crouch, ready to fight. The customer had laughed, but Kwame had stood up shaking, his face hot with shame. He started avoiding jobs that required basement work. He told his dispatcher he could only take residential calls where he could see the front door from his truck. His income dropped by half. His wife, who had been patient, began to worry openly about the bills. “You used to fix anything,” she said one evening, not cruelly, but the words sat in him like a stone. He had come to believe that he was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him—that the man who had calmly repaired burst pipes and soothed anxious homeowners was gone, replaced by someone who flinched at shadows and second-guessed every decision. When a leak required a decision about which valve to turn, Kwame would freeze, terrified of making the wrong choice. The self-doubt was constant: he could not trust that he would do the right thing, not even in the smallest repair.

The injustice of it all was a low, persistent hum in his mind. His attacker had faced no consequences. Kwame had done everything right—stayed calm, cooperated with the police, told the truth—and nothing had changed. The system that was supposed to protect him had let him down, and now he was the one who could not work, who could not sleep, who jumped at a sudden motion from his own wife when she came up behind him in the kitchen. He had stopped going to church, stopped visiting friends, stopped accepting invites to barbecues because the unpredictable movements of others felt like threats. What finally brought him to seek help was the morning he had to call his wife to come home from work because he could not open the front door to leave for a job. His hand had been on the knob for twenty minutes, the image of the crowbar flickering in his mind, and he had been certain that if he stepped outside something terrible would happen again. He sat in the hallway waiting for her, and when she arrived, he saw the fear in her eyes—not fear of him, but fear for him. He was hoping, now, to find a way back to the man who believed he could fix things. He was terrified that such a man no longer existed.
